**Generated by `scripts/compare_policies.py`. Do not edit by hand.**

- scenario: `line-a-one-shift`, 8 hours, 3 technicians

Every figure is a mean over the seeds. `docs/results/comparison.csv` holds each run, so the reading below can be checked rather than taken.

Read `README.md` in this directory first. It says what this is not.

## The gap, and what closes it

The column worth reading is not any single number but how the distance between the policies moves down the rows. ADR-021's claim is that a station's buffer decides what a stopped machine costs the line, so the advantage of a policy that knows about buffers might be expected to shrink as every station gets thicker ones. Whether it does is what this table is for; it is not assumed here, and the numbers below are reported whichever way they fall.

| buffer | 3A - 3C units lost | 3B - 3C units lost |
|---|---:|---:|
| as configured | -10.5 | +4.7 |
| 0 units | -9.3 | +4.1 |
| 5 units | -9.4 | +4.4 |
| 10 units | -8.1 | +6.2 |
| 20 units | -11.3 | +4.3 |
| 40 units | -15.2 | +2.5 |

A positive number means the baseline lost more production than the gate and score did; a negative one means it lost less. Averaged across the arrival multipliers, so this table is coarser than the ones above it and is a shape rather than a result.
